title: The 'Hello Dolly' album and 'Some Day'
summary: Moore explains the Las Vegas recordings in which he played 'Some Day', though Trummy Young is on 'Hello Dolly'.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: That was the same group that recorded

"Hello Dolly" album, you know, after "Hello Dolly" was originally recorded and then they filled it out with a number of selections, the Kapp record company and "I Still Get Jealous"/"Some Day", which was a specialty for you. "Hey Look Me Over," "Be my Life's Companion," "Jeepers-Creepers" "Moon River," You're a Woman, I'm a Man," "A Kiss to Build a Dream" those are the --
Yes, yes, but I might say this on that "Hello Dolly" tape, I'm not on it. It's Trummy Young that's on it.
Trummy is on "Hello Dolly," right. And he's on one other selection, I believe, "It's been a Long, Long Time," but you're on the rest of those.

The rest of those -- here's what happened. We were booked at The Riviera in Las Vegas and we were going to be there a month, so I took the whole family out there to Las Vegas, we had an apartment and during that week or during that month we made an album and they put that "Hello Dolly" album on this album along with the other things but on the "Hello Dolly" album was Trummy Young, but on all the rest there, I was on it. That's the way it is -- it was, you know. That's what made the album, "Hello Dolly." But they had recorded "Hello Dolly" earlier

It comes over very clearly on the album.

He knew, he's so great. He knew that I liked that. He came to me and said, "Chief, you like "Some Day" so much," we're going to cut this side and when I say, 'Take it, Chief, take it Chief,' you take a 15-bar solo then we'll go out. It knocked me out.

Yeah, you were in good form that session. You have some very pungent solos there, they were very strong, they swung and certainly there was a lot of the beat driving the music there. How did you feel about that record session?

Oh, it was beautiful, beautiful. We ran over quite a few tunes to record because we had some new arrangements, a couple of those tunes. It was nostalgic. Of course I hear some of these things that Louis had done before.
How many takes of "Some Day" did you do?
I think it was only one take.

Everybody was so -- see, when you do the same thing each night and every night, invariably when you make a record, it takes only one take, unless maybe for volume -- maybe the piano player is a little bit too loud or maybe too soft, so maybe you have to retake it, to tape it, you know. It's mostly the sound, the loudness and balance.

Otherwise you play the same thing over and over again. I venture to say that on all my engagements with Louie, with the small band, we played this so often, you know. Each one knows what to do and sometimes I have nightmares of the same thing all over and over and over, but what we did over and over and over, I never regretted it. I never regretted the nightmares because it was beautiful work with Louis that we were doing and what we did on the albums, we did it all the time, because that's the way people like us. That's the way the people liked Louie. Believe me, it was wonderful to work with Louie again.
